question: Explain scaled dot-product attention and why the dot product is divided by √dₖ.
answer:
Scaled dot‑product attention computes a weighted sum of the value vectors V for each query q.  
Given matrices of queries Q, keys K and values V, the attention output is

\[
\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V ,
\]

where \(d_k\) is the dimensionality of the key (and query) vectors [S1].

The dot products \(q\!\cdot\!k\) can grow large when the dimensionality \(d_k\) is high, because if the components of \(q\) and \(k\) are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, the variance of the dot product is \(d_k\) [S1]. Large dot‑product magnitudes push the softmax into its extreme tails, producing very small gradients and slowing learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) scales the dot products to have unit variance, keeping the softmax in a regime with stable gradients and improving training stability [S1].

3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention

We call our particular attention "Scaled Dot-Product Attention" (Figure 2). The input consists of
queries and keys of dimension dk, and values of dimension dv. We compute the dot products of the
query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the
values.

In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together
into a matrix Q. The keys and values are also packed together into matrices K and V . We compute
the matrix of outputs as:

Attention(Q, K, V ) = softmax(QKT )V (1) √dk

The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention [2], and dot-product (multiplicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to our algorithm, except for the scaling factor
of √dk1 . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with
a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is
much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized
matrix multiplication code.

While for small values of dk the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms
dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk [3]. We suspect that for large values of
dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has
extremely small gradients 4. To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by √dk1 .

question: Explain scaled dot-product attention and why the dot product is divided by √dₖ.
answer:
Scaled dot‑product attention computes a weighted sum of the value vectors \(V\) for each query \(q\).  
The weight assigned to each value is obtained by first taking the dot product of the query with every key \(k\), scaling the result, and then applying a softmax:

\[
\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V \quad [S1]
\]

The scaling factor \(\sqrt{d_{k}}\) is used to counteract the tendency of the raw dot products to grow large when the dimensionality \(d_{k}\) of the queries and keys is large.  When the components of \(q\) and \(k\) are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_{k}\); thus for large \(d_{k}\) the dot products can become large in magnitude, pushing the softmax into a region with extremely small gradients \([S1]\).  Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_{k}}\) brings the dot‑product values into a range where the softmax remains in a well‑behaved region, improving training stability and performance \([S1]\).
